questions.q: There are two wires of same material and same length while the diameter of second wire is two times the diameter of the first wire. Then the ratio of extensions produced in the wires by applying same load will be
questions.explanation: Extension = FL/(AY), with A ∝ d². Since d$_2$ = 2d$_1$, A$_2$ = 4A$_1$, so extension$_2$ = extension$_1$/4, giving the ratio extension$_1$:extension$_2$ = 4:1.

questions.q: Two wires A and B are made of same material. Their diameters are in the ratio of 1:2 and lengths are in the ratio of 1:3. If they are stretched by the same force, then increase in their lengths will be in the ratio of
A thick metal wire of density $\rho$ and length 'L' is hung from a rigid support. The increase in length of the wire due to its own weight is (Y=Young's modulus of the material of the wire)
questions.explanation: Treating the wire's own weight as acting effectively at its centre, the elongation is $\Delta L=\dfrac{mgL}{2AY}=\dfrac{\rho gL^2}{2Y}$.

questions.q: A stretched wire of a material whose Young's modulus Y = 2 × 10$^{11}$ Nm$^{-2}$ has Poisson's ratio 0.25. Its lateral strain $\varepsilon_l = 10^{-3}$. The elastic energy density of the wire is
questions.explanation: Longitudinal strain = lateral strain/Poisson's ratio = 10$^{-3}$/0.25 = 4×10$^{-3}$. Energy density = $\frac{1}{2}Y\varepsilon^2$ = 0.5×2×10$^{11}$×(4×10$^{-3}$)$^2$ = 1.6×10$^6$ Jm$^{-3}$.

questions.q: A metallic rod breaks when strain produced is 0.2%. The Young's modulus of the material of the rod is 7 $\times$ 10$^9$ N/m$^2$. The area of cross section to support a load of 10$^4$ N is
Young's modulus of a perfect rigid body is
questions.explanation: A perfectly rigid body undergoes no strain for any stress, so $Y=\text{stress/strain}\to\infty$.

questions.q: A wire is stretched such that its volume remains constant. The Poisson's ratio of the material of the wire is
questions.note: Volume conservation under stretching (isotropic wire) requires Poisson's ratio $\sigma = 0.5$ (i.e. 1-2\sigma=0), so the standard answer is option A (0.50), not B.
questions.explanation: The KEA key marks option B ($-$0.50) as correct.

questions.q: Two wires A and B are stretched by the same load. If the area of cross-section of wire 'A' is double that of 'B', then the stress on 'B' is
questions.explanation: Stress = F/A for the same load F. Since A$_A$ = 2A$_B$, stress on B = F/A$_B$ = 2(F/A$_A$) = twice the stress on A.

questions.q: 'Young's modulus' is defined as the ratio of
questions.explanation: Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of tensile (longitudinal) stress to longitudinal strain, valid within the elastic limit.

questions.q: A spring is stretched by applying a load to its free end. The strain produced in the spring is
questions.note: The standard textbook answer is that stretching a helical spring twists the wire, producing pure shear strain; the KEA key credits 'Longitudinal & Shear' instead.
questions.explanation: Stretching a helical spring twists the wire, producing shear strain in it, but the KEA key credits 'Longitudinal & Shear' strain.

questions.q: The ratio of hydraulic stress to the corresponding strain is known as
questions.explanation: By definition, the ratio of hydraulic (volume) stress to volumetric strain is the bulk modulus.

questions.q: The following four wires of length $L$ and radius $r$ are made of the same material. Which of these will have the largest extension, when the same tension is applied?
questions.explanation: Extension $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{\pi r^2 Y} \propto \dfrac{L}{r^2}$; computing $L/r^2$ for each option gives the largest value for $L=100$ cm, $r=0.2$ mm.

questions.q: Which of the following substances has the highest elasticity?
questions.explanation: Steel has the highest Young's modulus among the given materials, and hence the highest elasticity.
